title: My Father works (John 5:10–30)
hook: healing on the sabbath: my Father is working still, and so am I

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man thirty-eight years by the pool, and a question that wasn't as obvious as it sounded. Your line was do you want to be well? What step did you take? Day six hundred six.

The healed man is walking through Jerusalem with his rolled-up mat under his arm. It's the sabbath, the day of rest that Jewish law protects, and carrying a load through the city was one of the things the law set aside for that day. Some of the religious leaders stop him. You can't carry that today. And his answer is wonderfully human: the man who healed me told me to. Who was it? He doesn't know. He never got the name. Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus finds him in the temple. And now the question of the sabbath reaches Jesus himself.

When Jesus finds the man in the temple, he tells him: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." The man goes and tells the leaders who healed him. And the argument begins. Remember, this is a debate among Jews: Jesus, his disciples and his questioners all kept the sabbath and honored it. What they disagree about is what keeping it means. Jesus's answer is a single sentence: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." Hitherto means until now. My Father is still working, so I am too. Here's what makes that sentence so sharp. Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. Yet the world keeps going on the sabbath. Babies are born, rain falls, hearts beat. Jewish teachers of that era asked the same question: how can God rest, when the world needs holding up every moment? Some answered that God never stops sustaining the world, even on the sabbath. Jesus takes that thought and stands inside it. If the Father is still at work, the Son works with him. His listeners hear the claim clearly: he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then Jesus describes how it works between them: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do." Like an apprentice at a workbench, watching the master's hands and copying them. Christians across the churches read this passage as a key to who Jesus is: not a rival to God, but the Son doing exactly what the Father does. And it's also a picture of God that doesn't clock out. The work of healing, giving life and setting things right is still going on.
screen: then, large: `MY FATHER WORKETH HITHERTO, AND I WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good work today. Settle, and breathe. Notice what is working in you right now without any effort. Your heart beating. Your lungs filling. The ground holding you up. Then think of one good piece of work you could do today. Something that heals or helps, even a small thing: a message to someone lonely, a repair you've put off, carrying something for someone. Picture yourself doing it. If you pray, you can ask to see where God is already at work, and join in. If you don't, choose the work anyway. The bell holds the time.
My Father works. Jesus's answer when he healed on the sabbath: God is still at work, and the Son works with him.
Your line: god is still working. Today, do the one good work you chose, and look for one sign that healing is still going on around you. Day six hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians read this passage as a teaching about Jesus as the Son of God; many also see in it a call to join in God's ongoing work of healing and care.

original.note: Greek: he is working. My Father is working until now (John 5:17).

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was breaking the sabbath rules.
what it means: a debate among Jews about what rest means, and Jesus's answer: God never stops giving life, so neither does he.
what a scholar hears: Jewish thinkers like Philo also held that God's work of sustaining the world never ceases, and Jesus builds his claim on that thought.

notes: Carrying a burden on the sabbath: cf. Jeremiah 17:21–22 and later rabbinic rules (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists carrying among the forbidden labors). Confirm.

The claim that Jewish teachers asked how God could rest while sustaining the world, with Philo as an example (Leg. All. 1.5–6) and later rabbinic discussion (e.g., Genesis Rabbah 11:10): confirm citations.

The script frames the sabbath argument as an intra-Jewish debate and avoids 'the Jews persecuted Jesus' (5:16); the KJV uses 'the Jews', which in John often means the Judean authorities. Confirm framing.
Index carry is lowercase 'god is still working'; kept exactly.
